beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson six. Membrane potential, ion pumps, and cotransport. [[beet]]A sugar beet packs an enormous amount of sugar into its root. [[nerve]]A nerve cell sends signals along its whole length. [[cell]]Both depend on something invisible at the edge of their cells: an electric voltage. [[patch]]Back at our patch of membrane, [[lit]]the pumps and a cotransporter are lit today. Let's see what they do with electric charge.
beats.voltage: Every living cell is a tiny battery. [[ions]]There are ions on both sides of the membrane, some positive, some negative. [[uneven]]But they are not spread out evenly. Just inside the membrane there is a surplus of negative charge, and just outside, a surplus of positive charge. [[volt]]That difference in charge is a voltage, and the voltage across a membrane is called the membrane potential. [[meter]]It is measured in millivolts, thousandths of a volt. The textbook gives animal cells values from about minus fifty to minus two hundred millivolts, and the minus sign says the inside is negative. [[thin]]The extra charge sits in a thin layer along the two faces of the membrane. The fluid farther away stays neutral.
beats.forces: Now, what does that mean for an ion that wants to cross? [[chem]]It feels two pushes. The first is the chemical force, which is just the ion's concentration gradient, from crowded to sparse. [[elec]]The second is the electrical force, the effect of the membrane potential. Positive ions are pulled toward the negative inside, and negative ions are pushed away from it. [[comb]]Together, the two forces are called the electrochemical gradient, and it drives the diffusion of ions across a membrane. [[na]]Take a sodium ion. There is more sodium outside than inside, so the chemical force points in. The inside is negative, so the electrical force points in as well. Both agree, and the pull is strong. [[k]]A potassium ion is different. There is more potassium inside, so the chemical force points out, but the negative inside pulls it back in. When the forces disagree, the ion follows whichever force is stronger.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which way does each force push?
beats.pumps: So who builds this voltage? [[pump]]An electrogenic pump is a transport protein that generates voltage across a membrane. [[animal]]In animal cells, the major one is the sodium-potassium pump. You met it in lesson five. It moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in, so each cycle sends a little more positive charge out than in. [[plant]]In plants, fungi, and bacteria, the main electrogenic pump is a proton pump.
beats.proton: Here is the proton pump at work. [[atp]]It is powered by {{ATP|A T P}}. [[push]]It takes a hydrogen ion, which is just a proton, from the cytoplasm, and pushes it out into the extracellular fluid, against the gradient. [[charge]]Every proton that leaves takes one positive charge with it. Positive charge builds up outside, and negative charge is left behind inside. The membrane potential grows. [[store]]And that is stored energy. Protons crowded outside, pulled back by the negative inside, are like water behind a dam. The pump spends {{ATP|A T P}} to fill the dam, and the cell can spend the stored energy later, on cellular work.
beats.q2: Quick check. Why is the proton pump called electrogenic?
beats.cotrans: Which brings us to cotransport. [[def]]Cotransport happens when active transport of one solute indirectly drives the transport of another solute. [[plant]]Plants commonly use the hydrogen ion gradient made by proton pumps to bring nutrients into the cell. Take sucrose, the sugar our beet stores. [[cot]]In the membrane sits a sucrose, hydrogen ion cotransporter. [[h]]The protons crowded outside drift back in through it, down their electrochemical gradient. That is the dotted arrow on the slide, diffusion of hydrogen ions. [[suc]]But the cotransporter will not let a proton through alone. A sucrose molecule rides in with each proton, even when there is already more sucrose inside. [[ind]]So sucrose is carried uphill, and the cell never spends {{ATP|A T P}} on sucrose itself. The pump spent it on protons, and that is why we call this transport indirect.
beats.example: Let's follow the whole chain once. [[a]]{{ATP|A T P}} powers the proton pump. [[b]]The pump moves protons out, and builds a gradient and a voltage. [[c]]Protons flow back in through the cotransporter, carrying sucrose with them. [[d]]Sucrose piles up in the cell, which is how a sugar beet fills its root. [[block]]Now suppose a poison blocks the pump. The protons stop piling up, the voltage fades, and the cotransporter has no push left. Sucrose uptake slows, even though the cotransporter itself is fine.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Membrane potential is the voltage across a membrane, made by uneven ions, with the inside negative. [[w2]]An ion feels a chemical force and an electrical force, and together they are its electrochemical gradient. [[w3]]Electrogenic pumps make the voltage: the sodium-potassium pump in animals, the proton pump in plants, fungi, and bacteria. They store energy as a gradient. [[w4]]Cotransport lets that stored energy carry another solute, like sucrose, into the cell. [[end]]Now try the practice.
